claim: NIFK (MKI67IP) and Ki-67 (MKI67) RNA expression show a significantly positive correlation in almost all cancer types in the TCGA pan-cancer cohort.
source: In the TCGA pan-cancer cohort, significantly positive correlations between MKI67IP (NIFK) and MKI67 (Ki-67) RNA expression were observed in almost all cancer types.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA pan-cancer cohort data presented in Figure 1A showing correlation patterns across cancer types.

claim: Among cancer types with high MKI67IP expression, lung cancer exhibits the strongest correlation between MKI67IP and MKI67 expression (ρ = 0.488, p<0.001).
source: Among the cancer types that displayed high MKI67IP expression, lung cancer exhibited the strongest correlation between MKI67IP and MKI67 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of TCGA data showing correlation coefficient and p-value, presented in Figure 1A.

claim: NIFK protein expression is significantly higher in lung cancer tissue samples compared to paired normal tissue.
source: Based on IHC analysis, significant overexpression of NIFK compared with paired normal tissue was observed in lung cancer (upper)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis data presented in Figure 1B showing NIFK expression levels in paired samples.

claim: NIFK protein expression is significantly higher in colorectal cancer tissue samples compared to paired normal tissue.
source: Based on IHC analysis, significant overexpression of NIFK compared with paired normal tissue was observed in lung cancer (upper) and colorectal cancer (lower left)
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC analysis data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: NIFK protein expression is not significantly different between breast cancer tissue samples and paired normal tissue.
source: Based on IHC analysis, significant overexpression of NIFK compared with paired normal tissue was observed in lung cancer (upper) and colorectal cancer (lower left) but not in breast cancer (lower right).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC analysis data presented in Figure 1B showing no significant difference in breast cancer.

claim: High MKI67IP expression is associated with poor survival in lung, breast, and blood cancer.
source: High MKI67IP expression was associated with poor survival in several cancer types, including lung, breast, and blood cancer (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis from the PrognoScan database presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Lung cancer displays the highest hazard ratio for MKI67IP overexpression among various cancer types (hazard ratio = 4.71, Cox p value = 0.000308).
source: By ranking the hazard ratios from the Cox proportional hazards survival model, we determined that high MKI67IP expression corresponded to the highest hazard ratio in lung cancer patients (hazard ratio = 4.71, Cox p value = 0.000308).
evidence: The claim is supported by Cox proportional hazards survival model analysis presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Lung cancer patients with high NIFK protein expression exhibit more frequent nodal involvement (p = 0.032).
source: Based on clinicopathological analysis of lung cancer, the patients displaying high NIFK protein expression exhibited more frequent nodal involvement (p = 0.032)
evidence: The claim is supported by clinicopathological analysis data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Lung cancer patients with high NIFK protein expression exhibit more frequent distant metastasis (p = 0.036).
source: Based on clinicopathological analysis of lung cancer, the patients displaying high NIFK protein expression exhibited more frequent nodal involvement (p = 0.032) and distant metastasis (p = 0.036)
evidence: The claim is supported by clinicopathological analysis data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Lung cancer patients with high NIFK protein expression exhibit a higher pathological stage (p = 0.059).
source: Based on clinicopathological analysis of lung cancer, the patients displaying high NIFK protein expression exhibited more frequent nodal involvement (p = 0.032) and distant metastasis (p = 0.036), as well as a higher pathological stage (p = 0.059) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinicopathological analysis data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: NIFK overexpression significantly increases cell migration in A549 cells (p<0.001 for 4 MOI).
source: A significant increase in cell migration after NIFK overexpression was observed in the wound-healing assay (p<0.001 for 4 MOI, Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound-healing assay data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: NIFK overexpression increases cell migration and invasion in transwell assays.
source: Increased cell migration and invasion upon NIFK overexpression were confirmed by the transwell assay with short incubation time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell assay data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: H661 and H1299 cells were derived from metastatic sites in lung cancer patients.
source: In addition, higher endogenous NIFK levels were detected in H661 and H1299 cells, which were derived from metastatic sites in lung cancer patients (ATCC) and are considered to be invasive (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of ATCC cell line information.

claim: H661 and H1299 cells are considered to be invasive.
source: In addition, higher endogenous NIFK levels were detected in H661 and H1299 cells, which were derived from metastatic sites in lung cancer patients (ATCC) and are considered to be invasive (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on established characterization of these cell lines.

claim: NIFK knockdown inhibits cell migration in H661 and H1299 cells, especially in clone sh6 (p<0.01).
source: Cell migration was inhibited after NIFK knockdown, especially in clone sh6 (p<0.01, Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound-healing assay data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: NIFK overexpression increases lung metastasis in NSG mice injected with A549 cells (p = 0.0127).
source: Increased lung metastasis was observed in the NIFK-overexpressing group both grossly and microscopically (p = 0.0127, Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo animal model data presented in Figures 3B-C.

claim: NIFK silencing significantly reduces the number of metastatic lung nodules in H661 cell-injected mice (p = 0.0054).
source: Similarly, significantly reduced numbers of metastatic lung nodules were observed in the NIFK-silenced H661 cell-injected group (p = 0.0054)
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo animal model data presented in Figure 3D-E.

claim: NIFK silencing significantly reduces the number of metastatic lung nodules in H1299 cell-injected mice (p = 0.0169).
source: Similarly, significantly reduced numbers of metastatic lung nodules were observed in the NIFK-silenced H661 cell-injected group (p = 0.0054) and in the NIFK-silenced H1299 cell-injected group (p = 0.0169) compared with the corresponding non-silenced (NS) control cell-injected groups (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo animal model data presented in Figure 3D-E.

claim: High NIFK IHC expression significantly correlates with poor overall survival in the Taiwanese lung cancer cohort (p = 0.018).
source: In our patient cohort, high NIFK IHC expression significantly correlated with poor overall survival in both the Taiwanese (p = 0.018) and Korean (p = 0.041) lung cancer cohorts (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: High NIFK IHC expression significantly correlates with poor overall survival in the Korean lung cancer cohort (p = 0.041).
source: In our patient cohort, high NIFK IHC expression significantly correlated with poor overall survival in both the Taiwanese (p = 0.018) and Korean (p = 0.041) lung cancer cohorts (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: NIFK downregulation decreases cancer proliferation in H661 and H1299 cells at 96 hr in vitro.
source: NIFK downregulation in H661 and H1299 cells decreased the cancer proliferation at 96 hr in vitro (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: H1299 cells with NIFK silencing display reduced tumor weight in vivo (p<0.01).
source: Furthermore, H1299 cell with NIFK silencing displayed the reduced tumor weight and volume in vivo p<0.01, Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: H1299 cells with NIFK silencing display reduced tumor volume in vivo (p<0.01).
source: Furthermore, H1299 cell with NIFK silencing displayed the reduced tumor weight and volume in vivo p<0.01, Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Ki-67 silencing decreases cell growth in both A549 and PC13 cells.
source: The NIFK-regulated cell proliferation was Ki-67-dependent that Ki-67 silencing decreased cell growth in both A549 and PC13 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Both RRM and Ki-FHA binding domain are involved in NIFK-mediated tumor proliferation, with the Ki-FHA binding domain being more significant.
source: Based on Figure 4F, both RRM and Ki-FHA binding domain were involved in tumor proliferation, but the latter was more significant.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data with NIFK domain mutants presented in Figure 4F.

claim: High NIFK and Ki-67 expression correlates with poor survival in lung cancer patients at the protein level (p = 0.004).
source: In lung cancer cohort, we observed positive correlation of high NIFK/Ki-67 with poor survival at protein level (Figure 4G, p = 0.004)
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: NIFK and Ki-67 expression show significant positive correlation in lung cancer (p<0.001).
source: In lung cancer cohort, we observed positive correlation of high NIFK/Ki-67 with poor survival at protein level (Figure 4G, p = 0.004) and significant expression coefficient (Figure 4H, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: Ki-67 knockdown does not impact NIFK-induced cell migration in PC13 cells.
source: Knocking down Ki-67 expression by shRNA1 in NIFK-overexpressing PC13 cells and H1299 cells did not impact NIFK-induced cell migration or invasion (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell assay data presented in Figures 5A-D.

claim: Ki-67 knockdown does not impact NIFK-induced cell invasion in PC13 cells.
source: Knocking down Ki-67 expression by shRNA1 in NIFK-overexpressing PC13 cells and H1299 cells did not impact NIFK-induced cell migration or invasion (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell assay data presented in Figures 5A-D.

claim: Ki-67 knockdown does not impact NIFK-induced cell migration in H1299 cells.
source: Knocking down Ki-67 expression by shRNA1 in NIFK-overexpressing PC13 cells and H1299 cells did not impact NIFK-induced cell migration or invasion (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell assay data presented in Figures 5A-D.

claim: Ki-67 knockdown does not impact NIFK-induced cell invasion in H1299 cells.
source: Knocking down Ki-67 expression by shRNA1 in NIFK-overexpressing PC13 cells and H1299 cells did not impact NIFK-induced cell migration or invasion (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell assay data presented in Figures 5A-D.

claim: Wnt signaling is the most strongly affected pathway by NIFK overexpression based on MetaCore enrichment analysis.
source: Based on the MetaCore enrichment analysis, Wnt signaling, a previously identified pivotal pathway in regulating cancer metastasis was most strongly affected by NIFK overexpression (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by MetaCore pathway enrichment analysis of microarray data presented in Figures 5E-F.

claim: Wnt signaling is a previously identified pivotal pathway in regulating cancer metastasis.
source: Based on the MetaCore enrichment analysis, Wnt signaling, a previously identified pivotal pathway in regulating cancer metastasis was most strongly affected by NIFK overexpression (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from prior research.

claim: CK1α levels decrease following NIFK overexpression.
source: The levels of CK1α and the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC)-AXIN-CK1α-CTNNβ-GSK3β complex were decreased following NIFK overexpression, indicating that CK1α is a key molecule in the NIFK-regulated Wnt signaling pathway (Figure 5G–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray and Western blot data presented in Figures 5G-H.

claim: The APC-AXIN-CK1α-CTNNβ-GSK3β complex levels decrease following NIFK overexpression.
source: The levels of CK1α and the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC)-AXIN-CK1α-CTNNβ-GSK3β complex were decreased following NIFK overexpression, indicating that CK1α is a key molecule in the NIFK-regulated Wnt signaling pathway (Figure 5G–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray and pathway analysis data presented in Figures 5G-H.

claim: CK1α is a key molecule in the NIFK-regulated Wnt signaling pathway.
source: The levels of CK1α and the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC)-AXIN-CK1α-CTNNβ-GSK3β complex were decreased following NIFK overexpression, indicating that CK1α is a key molecule in the NIFK-regulated Wnt signaling pathway (Figure 5G–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed changes in CK1α and the destruction complex upon NIFK overexpression.

claim: NIFK overexpression increases the nuclear fraction of β-catenin.
source: The increased nuclear fraction of β-catenin was observed upon NIFK overexpression (Figure 5I)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis of nuclear fractions presented in Figure 5I.

claim: NIFK overexpression reduces β-catenin phosphorylation.
source: The increased nuclear fraction of β-catenin was observed upon NIFK overexpression (Figure 5I) as well as the reduced β-catenin phosphorylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: NIFK silencing decreases TCF/β-catenin transcriptional activity.
source: The results of TCF/β-catenin reporter assay revealed the decreased luciferase activity in the NIFK-silenced cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by TCF/β-catenin reporter assay data presented in Figure 5J.

claim: CK1α knockdown restores TCF/β-catenin transcriptional activity in NIFK-silenced H661 cells (p<0.01).
source: Additional knockdown of CK1α restored TCF/β-catenin transcriptional activity in both NIFK-silenced H661 and H1299 cells (p<0.01, Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCF/β-catenin reporter assay data presented in Figure 5J.

claim: CK1α knockdown restores TCF/β-catenin transcriptional activity in NIFK-silenced H1299 cells (p<0.01).
source: Additional knockdown of CK1α restored TCF/β-catenin transcriptional activity in both NIFK-silenced H661 and H1299 cells (p<0.01, Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCF/β-catenin reporter assay data presented in Figure 5J.

claim: TCF4, CD44, CCND1 and MMP7 are downstream transcriptional targets of TCF/β-catenin regulated by the NIFK-CK1α axis.
source: In addition, the downstream transcriptional targets of TCF/β-catenin, including TCF4, CD44, CCND1 and MMP7, were regulated by the NIFK-CK1α axis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: NIFK knockdown elicits CK1α upregulation in H661 and H1299 cell lines.
source: Knocking down NIFK expression elicited CK1α upregulation, which decreased the downstream inhibitory target β-catenin in the H661 and H1299 cell lines (Figure 6A, Left).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: NIFK knockdown decreases β-catenin levels in H661 and H1299 cell lines.
source: Knocking down NIFK expression elicited CK1α upregulation, which decreased the downstream inhibitory target β-catenin in the H661 and H1299 cell lines (Figure 6A, Left).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: NIFK overexpression using lentivirus decreases CK1α expression in A549 and PC13 cells.
source: In addition, NIFK overexpression using a lentivirus decreased CK1α expression and increased β-catenin level in A549 and PC13 cells (Figure 6A, Right).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: NIFK overexpression using lentivirus increases β-catenin levels in A549 and PC13 cells.
source: In addition, NIFK overexpression using a lentivirus decreased CK1α expression and increased β-catenin level in A549 and PC13 cells (Figure 6A, Right).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The CSNK1A1 promoter region from -969 to -127 bp is important for transcriptional activation.
source: The promoter region from -969 to -127 bp was found to be important for transcriptional activation, indicating the potential involvement of SRY and RUNX1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by promoter reporter assay data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: RUNX1 silencing decreases CK1α expression levels in H1299 cells.
source: Silencing of RUNX1 and SRY expression in H1299 cells using shRNA decreased the CK1α expression levels (Figure 6D)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: SRY silencing decreases CK1α expression levels in H1299 cells.
source: Silencing of RUNX1 and SRY expression in H1299 cells using shRNA decreased the CK1α expression levels (Figure 6D)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: CdxA knockdown does not change CK1α expression in H1299 cells.
source: whereas no change in CK1α expression was detected following knockdown of another putative transcription factor, CdxA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: NIFK silencing increases RUNX1 promoter binding in H1299 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, increased promoter binding of RUNX1 was observed in the NIFK-silenced H1299 cell clone sh6 compared with the NS control clone (Top panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: NIFK overexpression decreases RUNX1 promoter binding in PC13 cells.
source: In a complementary experiment, the overexpression of NIFK in PC13 cells decreased the promoter binding of RUNX1 (Figure 6E, Bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP assay data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: NIFK knockdown increases CK1 promoter activity in H1299 cells.
source: Our results revealed increased CK1 reporter activity after NIFK knockdown in H1299 cells, which was decreased by RUNX1 knockdown (p<0.001, Left, Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by promoter reporter assay data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: RUNX1 knockdown decreases CK1 promoter activity in NIFK-silenced H1299 cells (p<0.001).
source: Our results revealed increased CK1 reporter activity after NIFK knockdown in H1299 cells, which was decreased by RUNX1 knockdown (p<0.001, Left, Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by promoter reporter assay data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: NIFK overexpression dose-dependently decreases CK1 promoter activity in PC13 cells (p<0.001).
source: In addition, the relative luciferase activity was dose-dependently decreased by NIFK overexpression in PC13 cells (p<0.001, Right, Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by promoter reporter assay data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: RUNX1 mRNA level is destabilized upon NIFK overexpression.
source: Furthermore, RUNX1 mRNA level was found to be destabilized upon NIFK overexpression (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by actinomycin D chase assay data presented in Figures 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: NIFK overexpression decreases RUNX1 promoter activity.
source: Furthermore, RUNX1 mRNA level was found to be destabilized upon NIFK overexpression (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 3), and the promoter activity was decreased by NIFK (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by promoter reporter assay data presented in Figure 6H.

claim: RUNX1 is increased upon NIFK silencing.
source: Inversely, RUNX1 was increased upon NIFK silencing (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6I.

claim: NIFK and RUNX1 RNA levels are inversely correlated in the lung cancer cohort (p<0.001).
source: In the lung cancer cohort, the NIFK and RUNX1 or CK1α RNA levels were inversely correlated, whereas the RUNX1 and CK1α RNA expression levels were positively correlated (p<0.001, Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data presented in Figure 6J.

claim: NIFK and CK1α RNA levels are inversely correlated in the lung cancer cohort (p<0.001).
source: In the lung cancer cohort, the NIFK and RUNX1 or CK1α RNA levels were inversely correlated, whereas the RUNX1 and CK1α RNA expression levels were positively correlated (p<0.001, Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data presented in Figure 6J.

claim: RUNX1 and CK1α RNA expression levels are positively correlated in the lung cancer cohort (p<0.001).
source: In the lung cancer cohort, the NIFK and RUNX1 or CK1α RNA levels were inversely correlated, whereas the RUNX1 and CK1α RNA expression levels were positively correlated (p<0.001, Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data presented in Figure 6J.

claim: CK1α knockdown restores cell migration in NIFK-silenced H661 cells.
source: Knocking down CK1α expression restored cell migration compared with the NIFK knockdown-only group, although the effects on clones sh1 and sh2 were clearer than those on clone sh3 (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound-healing assay data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: CK1α knockdown restores cell migration in NIFK-silenced H1299 cells.
source: Knocking down CK1α expression restored cell migration compared with the NIFK knockdown-only group, although the effects on clones sh1 and sh2 were clearer than those on clone sh3 (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound-healing assay data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: CK1α knockdown significantly restores surface lung nodule formation in NIFK-silenced H661 cells.
source: The formation of surface lung nodules was significantly restored due to CK1α knockdown in the H661 and H1299 sh6 cells (Figure 7C–D, upper left).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo animal model data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: CK1α knockdown significantly restores surface lung nodule formation in NIFK-silenced H1299 cells.
source: The formation of surface lung nodules was significantly restored due to CK1α knockdown in the H661 and H1299 sh6 cells (Figure 7C–D, upper left).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo animal model data presented in Figure 7D.

claim: High levels of CK1α correlate with favorable prognosis in lung cancer patients (p = 0.051).
source: In support of this hypothesis, we observed that high levels of CK1α correlated with a favorable prognosis in lung cancer patients (p = 0.051) (Table 1 and Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis data presented in Table 1 and Figure 7E.

claim: The combination of NIFK (MKI67IP) and CK1α (CSNK1A1) represents a superior prognostic indicator for lung cancer (p = 0.01).
source: Furthermore, the combination of NIFK (MKI67IP) and CK1α (CSNK1A1) may represent a superior prognostic indicator for lung cancer (p = 0.01) (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: NIFK is a Ki-67-interacting protein.
source: Nucleolar protein interacting with the FHA domain of pKi-67 (NIFK) is a Ki-67-interacting protein.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Ki-67 is exclusively expressed in the nucleus during all active cell cycle phases (G1, S, G2, and mitosis) in actively proliferating cells but not in quiescent cells.
source: The finding that Ki-67 is exclusively expressed in the nucleus during all active cell cycle phases (G1, S, G2, and mitosis) in actively proliferating cells but not in quiescent cells renders it a reliable marker for proliferation fraction assessment (Gerdes et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gerdes et al., 1984.

claim: Ki-67 overexpression predicts poor prognosis in many cancer types including breast, lung, brain, and prostate cancer.
source: In many cancer types including breast (Luporsi et al., 2012), lung (Jakobsen and Sorensen, 2013), brain (Abry et al., 2010), and prostate cancer (Fisher et al., 2013), the Ki-67 expression level represents a proliferation index, and Ki-67 overexpression predicts poor prognosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Ki-67 has been used to determine cancer treatment strategies.
source: Moreover, Ki-67 has also been used to determine cancer treatment strategies (Dowsett et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dowsett et al., 2011.

claim: Ki-67 silencing elicits the disappearance of perichromosomal layers in mitosis and smaller nuclei of daughter cells leading to problems in mitosis.
source: Ki-67 silencing was recently reported to elicit the disappearance of perichromosomal layers in mitosis and the smaller nuclei of daughter cells leading to the problem in mitosis (Booth et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Booth et al., 2014.

claim: NIFK binds to the FHA domain of Ki-67 by two key regulators of mitosis: cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) and glycogen synthase kinase GSK-3.
source: NIFK binds to the FHA domain of Ki-67 by two key regulators of mitosis: cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) and glycogen synthase kinase GSK-3 (Byeon et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Byeon et al., 2005.

claim: NIFK sequential phosphorylation at Thr238 and Thr234 is required for Ki-67 interaction.
source: NIFK binds to the FHA domain of Ki-67 by two key regulators of mitosis: cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) and glycogen synthase kinase GSK-3 (Byeon et al., 2005), and the NIFK sequential phosphorylation at Thr238 and Thr234 is required for the Ki-67 interaction (Byeon et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Byeon et al., 2005.

claim: During mitosis, both NIFK and Ki-67 are recruited to the chromosome periphery.
source: During mitosis, both NIFK and Ki-67 are recruited to the chromosome periphery, and the localization of NIFK at the peripheral of mitotic chromosome is disrupted in the absence of Ki-67 (Booth et al., 2014; Van Hooser et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Booth et al., 2014 and Van Hooser et al., 2005.

claim: The localization of NIFK at the peripheral of mitotic chromosome is disrupted in the absence of Ki-67.
source: During mitosis, both NIFK and Ki-67 are recruited to the chromosome periphery, and the localization of NIFK at the peripheral of mitotic chromosome is disrupted in the absence of Ki-67 (Booth et al., 2014; Van Hooser et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Booth et al., 2014 and Van Hooser et al., 2005.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is critical during tumorigenesis and metastasis in various types of cancer.
source: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is critical during tumorigenesis and metastasis in various types of cancer (Polakis, 2000; Sinnberg et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Polakis, 2000 and Sinnberg et al., 2010.

claim: Stabilization and nuclear import of β-catenin activates downstream transcriptional targets MMP7, MYC, TCF4, CCND1 and CD44 which are related to cell cycle, differentiation and metastasis regulation.
source: Stabilization and nuclear import of β-catenin activates downstream transcriptional targets, MMP7, MYC, TCF4, CCND1 and CD44 which are related to cell cycle, differentiation and metastasis regulation (Schwartz et al., 2003; Dey et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schwartz et al., 2003, Dey et al., 2013, and Cho et al., 2011.

claim: Degradation of β-catenin is regulated via sequential phosphorylation by casein kinase 1α (CK1α) first, and then by GSK-3, which facilitates the formation of the destruction complex.
source: Degradation of β-catenin is shown to be regulated via sequential phosphorylation by casein kinase 1α (CK1α) first, and then by GSK-3, which facilitates the formation of the destruction complex (Hernandez et al., 2012; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hernandez et al., 2012 and Li et al., 2012.

claim: CK1 family members including CK1α are constitutively active in cells.
source: CK1 family members including CK1α are constitutively active in cells (Price MA, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Price MA, 2006.

claim: CK1α function is determined by its intracellular level.
source: CK1 family members including CK1α are constitutively active in cells (Price MA, 2006). Therefore, CK1α function is determined by its intracellular level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the constitutive activity of CK1α.

claim: NIFK was previously implicated as a c-Myc-responsive gene in breast cancer.
source: NIFK was previously implicated as a c-Myc-responsive gene in breast cancer (Musgrove et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Musgrove et al., 2008.

claim: Ki-67 has been demonstrated to be associated with metastasis and lymphovascular invasion in cancer patients.
source: Furthermore, aside from its role as a proliferation marker, Ki-67 has been demonstrated to be associated with metastasis and lymphovascular invasion in cancer patients (Pollack et al., 2004; Inwald et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pollack et al., 2004 and Inwald et al., 2013.

claim: CK1α is characterized as a negative regulator that blocks Wnt signaling pathway-mediated metastasis.
source: CK1α, a component of the β-catenin destruction complex, is characterized as a negative regulator that blocks Wnt signaling pathway-mediated metastasis (Clevers, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Clevers, 2006.

claim: The level of intracellular β-catenin is modulated by proteasomal degradation mediated by destruction complex, which is composed of APC, Axin, CK1α, and GSK3β.
source: In the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, the level of intracellular β-catenin is modulated by proteasomal degradation mediated by destruction complex, which is composed of APC, Axin, CK1α, and GSK3β (MacDonald et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to MacDonald et al., 2009.

claim: β-catenin and APC mutation is less commonly observed in lung cancer than in other cancer types such as colon cancer.
source: Given that β-catenin and APC mutation is less commonly observed in lung cancer than in other cancer types such as colon cancer, understanding the mechanism by which these Wnt signaling inhibitors regulate the β-catenin destruction complex is crucial (Stewart, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stewart, 2014.

claim: Downregulation of the members of the β-catenin destruction complex, including CK1α, is commonly observed in lung cancer cell lines and cancer tissue and correlates with poor prognosis or poor clinicopathological characteristics.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that the downregulation of the members of the β-catenin destruction complex, including CK1α, is commonly observed in lung cancer cell lines and cancer tissue and correlates with poor prognosis or poor clinicopathological characteristics (Yang et al., 2013; Srivastava et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2013, Srivastava et al., 2012, and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: A negative feedback loop of Wnt signaling activation was recently reported via the Huwe-1-dependent ubiquitylation of Dishevelled (Dvl).
source: Recently, a negative feedback loop of Wnt signaling activation was reported via the Huwe-1-dependent ubiquitylation of Dishevelled (Dvl) (de Groot et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to de Groot et al., 2014.

claim: Upon Wnt signaling activation, Dvl recruits Axin and GSK3-β away from the destruction complex, thereby inhibiting β-catenin destruction complex formation and, subsequently, β-catenin degradation.
source: Upon Wnt signaling activation, Dvl recruits Axin and GSK3-β away from the destruction complex, thereby inhibiting β-catenin destruction complex formation and, subsequently, β-catenin degradation (de Groot et al., 2014; Stambolic et al., 1996; Behrens et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to de Groot et al., 2014, Stambolic et al., 1996, and Behrens et al., 1998.

claim: Significant Huwe-1 upregulation was detected based on the microarray data of NIFK overexpression.
source: Correspondingly, we detected significant Huwe-1 upregulation based on the microarray data of NIFK overexpression, suggesting the activation of an alternative negative feedback loop via the decrease in Dvl activity (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data presented in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: CK1α plays a role as a tumor suppressor in p53-inactivated cancer cells.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that CK1α plays a role as a tumor suppressor in p53-inactivated cancer cells (Elyada et al., 2011; Huart et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elyada et al., 2011, Huart et al., 2009, and Chen et al., 2005.

claim: The loss of heterozygosity of CK1α results in highly invasive carcinoma in a p53-deficient mouse model.
source: The loss of heterozygosity of CK1α results in highly invasive carcinoma in a p53-deficient mouse model (Elyada et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Elyada et al., 2011.

claim: p53 inactivation is a major pathogenic event in lung cancer.
source: Because p53 inactivation is a major pathogenic event in lung cancer (Herbst et al., 2008), further research is necessary to determine the role of NIFK-mediated CK1α expression in p53-deficient lung cancer.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herbst et al., 2008.

claim: RUNX1 was originally recognized to display tumor-suppressive ability due to its role in acute myeloid leukemia tumorigenesis.
source: RUNX1 was originally recognized to display tumor-suppressive ability due to its role in acute myeloid leukemia tumorigenesis (Miyoshi et al., 1991; Silva et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miyoshi et al., 1991 and Silva et al., 2003.

claim: The loss of RUNX1 from intestinal epithelial cells significantly induced tumorigenesis in a conditional knockout mouse model.
source: The loss of RUNX1 from intestinal epithelial cells significantly induced tumorigenesis in a conditional knockout mouse model (Fijneman et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fijneman et al., 2012.

claim: The knockdown of RUNX1 in breast cancer cells resulted in hyperproliferation and abnormal morphogenesis.
source: The loss of RUNX1 from intestinal epithelial cells significantly induced tumorigenesis in a conditional knockout mouse model (Fijneman et al., 2012), and the knockdown of RUNX1 in breast cancer cells resulted in hyperproliferation and abnormal morphogenesis (Wang et al., 2011; Janes, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2011 and Janes, 2011.

claim: NIFK promotes lung cancer progression via RUNX1-dependent CK1α repression, which activates TCF4/β-catenin signaling in metastasis.
source: Our results demonstrate the prognostic value of NIFK, and suggest that NIFK is required for lung cancer progression via the RUNX1-dependent CK1α repression, which activates TCF4/β-catenin signaling in metastasis and the Ki-67-dependent regulation in cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data including in vitro and in vivo studies showing the NIFK-RUNX1-CK1α-β-catenin axis.

claim: NIFK promotes lung cancer progression via Ki-67-dependent regulation in cell proliferation.
source: Our results demonstrate the prognostic value of NIFK, and suggest that NIFK is required for lung cancer progression via the RUNX1-dependent CK1α repression, which activates TCF4/β-catenin signaling in metastasis and the Ki-67-dependent regulation in cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing NIFK-Ki-67 interaction effects on proliferation.

claim: NIFK is a promising therapeutic target for lung cancer patients.
source: Our study indicates that NIFK expression promotes cancer metastasis and proliferation leading to poor clinical outcomes; thus, NIFK may represent a prognostic indicator and a promising therapeutic target for lung cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the demonstrated role of NIFK in cancer progression.

claim: NIFK may represent a prognostic indicator for lung cancer patients.
source: Our study indicates that NIFK expression promotes cancer metastasis and proliferation leading to poor clinical outcomes; thus, NIFK may represent a prognostic indicator and a promising therapeutic target for lung cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical data showing correlation between NIFK expression and patient outcomes.
